mula_devanagari: इदं शरीरं कौन्तेय क्षेत्रम् इत्य् अभिधीयते | एतद् यो वेत्ति तं प्राहुः क्षेत्रज्ञ इति तद्-विदः
mula_iast: idaṃ śarīraṃ kaunteya kṣetram ity abhidhīyate | etad yo vetti taṃ prāhuḥ kṣetrajña iti tad-vidaḥ
jayatirtha_prameyadipika: ।।13.2।।पूर्वसङ्गतत्वेनाध्यायप्रतिपाद्यं दर्शयति -- पूर्वोक्ते ति। पूर्वमाषष्ठसमाप्तेर्यत् ज्ञानं ज्ञानसाधनमुक्तम्? यच्च सप्तमादिभिः षड्भिर्ज्ञेयं ब्रह्मस्वरूपमुक्तम्? यदपिभूमिरापः [7।4] इत्यादिना क्षेत्रमुक्तम्? यच्चन त्वेवाहं [2।12] इत्यादिना पुरुषभेद उक्तः? तत्सर्वमनेनाध्यायेन दर्शयति भगवान्। किमर्थं पिण्डीकृत्य विक्षिप्तमेकीकृत्य। गौणोऽत्र क्त्वाप्रत्ययः पिण्डीकरणार्थमित्यर्थः। पिण्डीकरणे मिश्रत्वादप्रतिपत्तिरेवेत्यत उक्तम् -- विविच्ये ति। प्रकरणशुद्ध्येत्यर्थः।

current_dvaita_rendering.english: Salutation to the giver of knowledge. In this chapter the Lord gathers into one the jñāna (knowledge), jñeya (the knowable), kṣetra (field) and puruṣa (person) taught earlier, and sets them out each distinguished from the others.
current_dvaita_rendering.divergence_note: THIN. The Madhva text supplied (his 13.2) is only a one-line chapter introduction; it glosses no word of this verse, not kṣetra, not kṣetrajña, not tad-vidaḥ. The one doctrinal signal is the emphasis on viveka (setting the four apart), which fits Dvaita but is not developed here. The rendering above translates the introduction itself, not a Dvaita reading of the verse, which the source does not supply.

current_dvaita_everyday: The commentary here only announces the chapter's method: take four things that were mixed together and set each out separately. A founder facing a messy crisis can start the same way, putting the product, the customer, the team and the money in separate columns before deciding anything. Nothing more specific can honestly be drawn from Madhva on this verse.

other_schools_english.advaita: This body, O Kaunteya, is called kṣetra (field): because it wastes, decays and perishes, or because the fruit of action is harvested in it as in a field. Whoever makes it an object of his knowing, from the soles of the feet to the crown, by native knowing or by instruction, and discerns it part by part, him the knowers of the two call kṣetrajña (knower of the field). Is field and knower known by this much alone? No; what more is to be known is now taught.
other_schools_english.viśiṣṭādvaita: This body, which a man speaks of in one breath with himself ('I am a god, I am a man, I am stout, I am lean'), is still other than the self who enjoys, and those who know the body truly call it the kṣetra (field) of that self's bhoga (experience); he who knows it, limb by limb and as a whole, as 'this I know' is, by being the knower, other than the known, and the knowers of the self call him kṣetrajña. We rightly say 'I am a man' only because the body exists solely as the self's viśeṣaṇa (mode), inseparable from it (apṛthak-siddhi), as cowness is from the cow. The knower's own form is not reached by the eye but by a mind refined in yoga; the deluded, standing near prakṛti (matter), see the knower in the shape of prakṛti, as I shall say in 15.10.
other_schools_english.śuddhādvaita: This body, a transformation of the prakṛti already called not-self (anātman), is named kṣetra (field) because it is the dwelling of the puruṣa, as is the great cosmos, so is the small body. So long as the puruṣa does not know it as distinct he is only kṣetrin (holder of the field) and remains in saṃsāra (the round of birth and death); whoever knows the field apart, and himself as its seer, him the knowers call kṣetrajña (knower of the field). Even in saṃsāra there is some knowing of field and knower, but blurred into one; this separateness belongs to the one who knows himself as kṣetrajña, not to all.
other_schools_english.bhakti: I promised to lift my devotees out of the sea of death and saṃsāra (rebirth), and that cannot happen without knowledge of the self; so now I teach the discrimination of prakṛti (nature) and puruṣa (person), the two natures, lower and higher, named in the seventh chapter. This body, the bhogāyatana (house of experience), is called kṣetra (field) because it is the ground where saṃsāra sprouts; he who 'knows' it, that is, takes it as 'I' and 'mine', is called kṣetrajña, because like a farmer he eats its harvest. So say the tad-vidaḥ, those who know how field and knower are told apart.
other_schools_english.advaita-bhakti: This body with its senses and inner organ, O Kaunteya, is called kṣetra (field), for in it the fruit of action ripens again and again like grain; whoever takes it as 'I' and 'mine' is called kṣetrajña (knower of the field), a farmer eating his own harvest. Mark the grammar: the field is named in the passive, as object, because it is inert, while 'kṣetrajña' stands with 'iti' and not as an object at all, because it is svaprakāśa (self-luminous); anyone may name the field, but only the vivekin (discerning) name its knower. This whole last hexad serves the meaning of the great sentence: that the kṣetrajña, one and changeless in every field, is not other than the non-dual paramātman (supreme self).
